data.title: Staff and Organisational Detail Supports Targeted Pretexts
data.summary: Publicly available sources provided a detailed picture of staff, reporting lines, internal systems and current projects — sufficient to construct pretexts that are specific, timely and credible to the people targeted.
data.description:
Pretexts fail on detail and succeed on it. The information that makes a request believable is rarely confidential: professional networking profiles give names, roles and reporting lines; job advertisements name the exact technologies and versions in use; press releases and social posts announce projects, acquisitions and travel; and conference talks reveal internal architecture.

Assembled, this supports a message that names a real project, a real manager and a real system, sent while the person named is genuinely away — which is far more convincing than any technical trick.

Photographs are a specific and underestimated source. Pictures taken in offices disclose badge designs and numbers, screens, whiteboards, desk layouts and door hardware, and are published by the organisation itself in recruitment material.
data.recommendation:
* Review what the organisation publishes about staff, systems and projects, and reduce unnecessary specificity — particularly technology versions in job adverts.
* Brief high-exposure roles — executives, finance, service desk, IT administrators — on how their public profile is used against them.
* Check photographs for badges, screens and whiteboards before publication.
* Monitor for look-alike domains and for impersonation profiles on social platforms.
* Accept that this cannot be eliminated, and make verification processes strong enough that credible pretexts still fail.
data.short_recommendation: Reduce published detail and brief high-exposure roles.
